evidence.claim: North through a wildlife corridor to a ferry town and border crossing.
evidence.quote: Highway 2/95 from  Sandpoint to Bonners Ferry runs through the corridor.

evidence.claim: North through a wildlife corridor to a ferry town and border crossing.
evidence.quote: The route serves as a connector between Bonners Ferry, via US-95 south, Porthill, and Creston, BC.

evidence.claim: North through a wildlife corridor to a ferry town and border crossing.
evidence.quote: Edwin Bonner, a merchant from Walla Walla, Washington, established a ferry in 1864 where the trail crossed the broad Kootenai River.

evidence.claim: Sandpoint stands on Lake Pend Oreille, surrounded by the Selkirk, Cabinet and Bitterroot mountain ranges.
evidence.quote: Sandpoint lies on the shores of Idaho's largest lake, 43-mile-long (69-kilometer) Lake Pend Oreille, and is surrounded by three major mountain ranges, the Selkirk, Cabinet and Bitterroot ranges.

evidence.claim: North of town, US 95 crosses the McArthur Lake Wildlife Corridor on its way to Bonners Ferry.
evidence.quote: Highway 2/95 from  Sandpoint to Bonners Ferry runs through the corridor.

evidence.claim: Conifer forests, wetlands, streams and rivers form the corridor’s landscape.
evidence.quote: It contains conifer forests, forested or shrub wetlands and swamps, streams and rivers.

evidence.claim: Farther north, State Highway 1 connects US 95 east of Copeland with Porthill on the Canadian boundary.
evidence.quote: It extends 11.185 miles (18.00 km) from U.S. Route 95 (US-95) east of Copeland, north to British Columbia Highway 21 (BC 21) in Porthill.

evidence.claim: US 95 bypasses downtown Sandpoint on a divided highway along the waterfront; at McArthur Lake, the road runs beside the reservoir’s east shore.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 95 travels north–south and bypasses downtown Sandpoint using a divided highway on the waterfront

evidence.claim: US 95 bypasses downtown Sandpoint on a divided highway along the waterfront; at McArthur Lake, the road runs beside the reservoir’s east shore.
evidence.quote: Highway 2/95 from Sandpoint to Bonners Ferry runs past the east shore.

evidence.claim: The historic Wildhorse Trail carried thousands of prospectors north after gold was discovered in British Columbia’s East Kootenays in 1863.
evidence.quote: When gold was discovered in the East Kootenays of British Columbia in 1863, thousands of prospectors from all over the West surged northward over a route that became known as the Wildhorse Trail.

evidence.claim: The following year, Walla Walla merchant Edwin Bonner established a ferry where that trail crossed the Kootenai River.
evidence.quote: Edwin Bonner, a merchant from Walla Walla, Washington, established a ferry in 1864 where the trail crossed the broad Kootenai River.

evidence.claim: The numbered highway came later: State Highway 1 developed from the 1920s Sampson Trail B and entered Idaho’s new numbering system in the mid-1930s.
evidence.quote: SH-1 was originally created in the 1920s as part of Sampson Trail B, which ran from Boise north to Lewiston, Coeur d'Alene, before entering British Columbia at Porthill. Later in the mid-1930s, Idaho adopted a new numbered highway system with SH-1 as one of the first highways.

evidence.claim: Travel north from Sandpoint on US 95, passing the east shore of McArthur Lake before Bonners Ferry.
evidence.quote: Highway 2/95 from Sandpoint to Bonners Ferry runs past the east shore.

evidence.claim: Beyond Bonners Ferry, State Highway 1 branches from US 95 east of Copeland and leads to Porthill.
evidence.quote: The route links Bonners Ferry, via US-95 south, Porthill, and Creston, BC.

evidence.claim: Beyond Bonners Ferry, State Highway 1 branches from US 95 east of Copeland and leads to Porthill
evidence.quote: The highway starts at an intersection with US-95 east of Copeland.

evidence.claim: At the border, it meets British Columbia Highway 21; the north-flowing Kootenai River lies just west of Porthill.
evidence.quote: Idaho State Highway 1 on the American side joins British Columbia Highway 21 on the Canadian side, which continues north towards Creston.

evidence.claim: At the border, it meets British Columbia Highway 21; the north-flowing Kootenai River lies just west of Porthill.
evidence.quote: The north-flowing Kootenai River is just west of Porthill.

evidence.claim: The highway crosses a route used by grizzly bears moving between the Selkirk and Cabinet mountains.
evidence.quote: It links the wilderness areas of the Selkirk and Cabinet mountains, and is used by species such as grizzly bears that move between these areas.

evidence.claim: Deer and other hoofed animals also winter here.
evidence.quote: It also provides a wintering area for deer and other ungulates.

evidence.claim: A highway, two railway lines, buildings and fences share the corridor with that movement.
evidence.quote: A highway and two railway lines run through the corridor, with a strip of side roads, buildings and fences along the highway.

evidence.claim: The highway has high rates of wildlife collisions, and difficult terrain limits options for safe crossings.
evidence.quote: The highway section running through the corridor has high rates of vehicle collisions with wildlife. There is limited opportunity for creating safe wildlife crossings due to the difficult terrain.

evidence.claim: Conservation groups have obtained easements on timberland to restrict further development while allowing sustainable forestry.
evidence.quote: Conservation groups have been active in obtaining easements on timber land to prevent further development in the corridor while allowing sustainable forestry.

evidence.claim: In September 2016, about 5,568 acres of forest east of McArthur Lake received conservation easements limiting development and subdivision while retaining forestry.
evidence.quote: In September 2016 about 5,568 acres (2,253 ha) of forest to the east of McArthur Lake between Sandpoint and Bonners Ferry was placed under conservation easements, which compensate landowners for limiting uses such as development and subdivision, but allow sustainable forestry to continue.

evidence.claim: Brick buildings on Main Street belong to a town that once perched on stilts against spring floods.
evidence.quote: The downtown took shape as brick buildings were constructed, replacing those on stilts.

evidence.claim: Brick buildings on Main Street belong to a town that once perched on stilts against spring floods.
evidence.quote: Bonners Ferry, perched on stilts to avoid the inevitable spring floods

evidence.claim: Bonners Ferry grew at the Kootenai River crossing established by Edwin Bonner in 1864.
evidence.quote: Edwin Bonner, a merchant from Walla Walla, Washington, established a ferry in 1864 where the trail crossed the broad Kootenai River.

evidence.claim: Richard Fry and his Sinixt wife, Justine Su-steel Fry, leased the ferry business in 1875, but Bonner’s name remained.
evidence.quote: In 1875, Richard Fry, and his Sinixt wife, Justine Su-steel Fry, leased the business, but the location retained the name of the original founder and later became the town of Bonners Ferry.

evidence.claim: As the town became a lumbering and farming center, valley land was drained and levees were built.
evidence.quote: Moving into the 20th century, the town became the center of a lumbering and farming community. The valley land was drained, levees were constructed

evidence.claim: Much of Main Street dates from the period when brick replaced the stilt-supported buildings.
evidence.quote: Today, much of Main Street dates from this initial period of solid, permanent construction.

evidence.claim: Completion of Libby Dam in 1975 reduced the threat of serious flooding, another change in the town’s relationship with the river.
evidence.quote: Completion of the Libby Dam in 1975 lessened the threat of serious flooding.

evidence.claim: The border settlement was once called Ockonook, meaning “a grassy hillside with rocks.”
evidence.quote: The former US name was Ockonook, meaning "a grassy hillside with rocks."

evidence.claim: Charles Plummer Hill took over as its US customs officer in 1893.
evidence.quote: Charles Plummer Hill took over as the US customs officer, a position he held for 10 years.

evidence.claim: Charles Plummer Hill took over as its US customs officer in 1893.
evidence.quote: Major Joseph I. Barnes was the US inspector of customs until the end of Benjamin Harrison's presidential term in 1893. That year, Barnes became the inaugural US postmaster at Ockonook.

evidence.claim: As postmaster in 1897, he succeeded in renaming the settlement Porthill.
evidence.quote: That year, as postmaster, Hill succeeded in renaming the settlement Porthill

evidence.claim: As postmaster in 1897, he succeeded in renaming the settlement Porthill.
evidence.quote: By 1897, J.I. Barnes also ran a general store. That year, McLoughlin received a land patent

evidence.claim: The border buildings changed too: in 1967, the United States replaced its 1938 brick station with a wooden structure in a different location.
evidence.quote: In 1967, the US replaced its 1938 brick border station with the current wooden structure. A redesign of the road approach positioned the new facility in a different location, preserving the former building.

evidence.claim: The earlier building was preserved and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2014.
evidence.quote: In 2014, the old border station was added to the National Register of Historic Places listings in Boundary County, Idaho.

evidence.claim: The north-flowing Kootenai River lies west of town; at the crossing, Idaho Highway 1 joins British Columbia Highway 21 toward Creston.
evidence.quote: The north-flowing Kootenai River is just west of Porthill.

evidence.claim: The north-flowing Kootenai River lies west of town; at the crossing, Idaho Highway 1 joins British Columbia Highway 21 toward Creston.
evidence.quote: Idaho State Highway 1 on the American side joins British Columbia Highway 21 on the Canadian side, which continues north towards Creston.
